title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
publication_status_observed: ICML 2017 proceedings (34th International Conference on Machine Learning, Sydney)
main_claims: Most standard notions of flatness (volume epsilon-flatness, Hessian spectral norm, epsilon-sharpness) are problematic for deep rectifier networks because the non-negative homogeneity of ReLU activations allows construction of observationally equivalent parameters with arbitrarily sharper or flatter loss surfaces.

Reparametrisation of the function (e.g., weight normalisation, batch normalisation) can change the geometry of the loss landscape drastically without affecting the function's generalisation properties.
Flatness as commonly measured cannot be used directly to explain or predict generalisation in deep networks without first specifying and justifying a particular parametrisation.
methodology: The paper presents theoretical arguments using alpha-scale transformations of a single hidden-layer rectifier network to show that every minimum is observationally equivalent to a minimum with arbitrarily large Hessian spectral norm or arbitrarily small epsilon-sharpness. Proofs are given for volume epsilon-flatness (Theorem 2), Hessian-based measures (Theorems 3-5), and epsilon-sharpness (Section 4.3), and analogous results for reparametrised functions are derived in Section 5.
key_results: For any deep rectifier network, every non-constant minimum has infinite volume epsilon-flatness (Theorem 2), rendering that measure uninformative for comparing generalisability.

For any minimum with non-zero Hessian, there exists an observationally equivalent parametrisation with arbitrarily large spectral norm of the Hessian, so sharpness defined by spectral norm is not parametrisation-invariant.

With weight normalisation reparametrisation, every minimum is observationally equivalent to both an infinitely sharp minimum and an infinitely flat minimum, further undermining flatness-based generalization arguments.
limitations: The counter-examples rely on specific scale symmetries of ReLU networks; the argument may not extend directly to architectures without such symmetries (e.g., batch-normalised networks where the symmetry is broken differently).
The paper does not provide empirical evidence that the constructed sharp-but-equivalent parametrisations are ever visited by gradient-based optimisers in practice.
The analysis focuses on 0-1 loss KL-divergence arguments from Hochreiter & Schmidhuber; more recent PAC-Bayes bounds with KL-invariant measures are not refuted.
relevance_to_rq: This is a foundational counter-argument to flatness-based explanations of generalisation, directly motivating the RQ's scepticism that sharpness alone explains SAM's OOD gains and supporting the need for complementary representation-stability measures like CKA.
